en: The Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One, Part Eight:
The Eight Pairs and Sixteen Classes of Disciples, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian. 1.
The Sūtra of King Jetaṃgha. The First Sūtra: The Sūtra of King Jetaṃgha.
Thus have I heard:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin.
In the Jeta Grove there was a large rice field that had ripened and was due for harvest by morning or evening.

A brahmin rose early in the morning and went to the field; seeing the stalks of grain from afar, his heart was filled with joy, and thinking he had achieved his wish, he gazed at the rice and could not bear to leave.
At that time, the Buddha, accompanied by the bhikṣus, entered the city to seek alms. Seeing from afar the brahmin’s joy and delight in this manner, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you all see this brahmin?"
They all replied, "We have seen him.
The Buddha remained silent and entered the city; after his meal, they each returned to their respective monasteries.
That very night, it rained large hailstones that destroyed all the grain in the fields.
A daughter of the brahmin also died that same night.
Because of these events, the brahmin was overwhelmed with grief and distress; he wept so bitterly that no one could stop him.

The next day, as the bhikṣus entered the city with their alms-bowls to seek food, they heard that the brahmin was suffering such a calamity and was weeping most piteously—a grief that neither śramaṇas, brahmins, nor any of the country’s people were able to dispel.
When the bhikṣu had finished eating, he returned to where the Buddha was, paid his respects, and said:
"The state of the brahmin’s mind was such as this.
As soon as he had finished speaking, the brahmin came weeping to where the Buddha was; after having greeted the Buddha, he sat down beside him.
The Buddha, knowing the root of his anxiety and what he was contemplating, immediately said to the brahmin:
"In the world there are five things that cannot be avoided, and from which no one can escape."
What are these five?
It is impossible to prevent the decline of that which is destined to decline;
it is impossible to prevent the loss of that which is destined to be lost.
When one is subject to the law of illness and emaciation, it is impossible to prevent being ill and emaciated;
when one is subject to the law of aging and decay, it is impossible to prevent aging and decay;
when one is subject to the law of death and departure, it is impossible to prevent death and departure.

"Ordinary people, lacking the Way and lacking wise discernment, when they see the phenomena of decay, loss, old age, sickness, and death arrive, immediately give rise to anxiety, distress, and lamentation; they beat their thighs and heat themselves, exhausting their bodies to no avail."
Why is this? Because one who sits does not hear or know the Truths; it should be thus, O Brahmin!
I have heard that those who embrace the Truth do not become distressed when they see the phenomena of decline, loss, abandonment, old age, sickness, and death approaching. Why is this?
Having heard and understood the Truths, it should be thus:
"It is not only my household that suffers decline; the world is likewise.
Since the world arises together with decline, how could I alone escape it?"

With a wise mind, I reflect with earnest deliberation: "I am now already diminished to such an extent that it causes me grief; sitting here emaciated and refusing food, my face has lost its luster. This brings joy to those who were my enemies and causes those who were close to me to grieve in my stead. My household affairs have fallen into ruin and neglected, and this depletion cannot be recovered."
"Having realized this as it truly is, when one sees the phenomena of decay, loss, old age, sickness, and death approaching, one will never again be distressed.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke these verses for the brahmin:
"With a voice of sorrow and lamentation, Can one recover even a fraction of what was lost before?"
Sorrow and grief are of no avail; they only bring joy to the hearts of one's enemies.
Those who possess sincerity and the discernment of truth do not grieve over old age, sickness, or death.
As for those who seek pleasure, it instead gives rise to affliction when they behold the beauty of blooming flowers.
The sound of flight cannot reach impermanence; seek immortality through precious jewels.
Knowing that once gone there is no returning, do not grieve for what is pursued; cultivate mindfulness and conduct to attain the supreme treasure of the world.
Know clearly that this cannot be pursued; as it is for the world, so it is for me and you.
Cast far away grief and anxiety, and practice right conduct; what benefit would there be in grieving over this world?

The Buddha further expounded the Dharma extensively for the brahmin; he then spoke of generosity and the observance of precepts, manifesting the path to the heavens and the desire for goodness, [showing that] evil is not firm or enduring.
The Buddha, knowing that the brahmin’s mind had become supple and was turning toward the Right Path, enabled him to perceive the Four Noble Truths.
With his mind liberated, the brahmin immediately attained the first stage of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), just as a clean, pure silk cloth readily takes on the color it is dyed with.
He immediately rose, placed his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and said:
"I have now seen the Truth, as if looking at my own reflection in a mirror.

From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Sangha of Bhikṣus. Accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who upholds the five precepts, remaining pure and unviolating of them for as long as life shall last."
He then rose, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.
The bhikṣus then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How wonderful!”
When the brahmin Khaṇḍadravya’s mind was thus resolved, he departed with a joyful smile.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“It is not only this brahmin’s grief that has been dispelled.”
In the distant past, there were five kings in this land of Jambudvīpa.
One of these kings was named Jietan (Jie-tan); he governed the state unjustly, and the ministers and the people all grew weary of his conduct. They gathered together for consultation and said:
"Let each of our families send forth soldiers."
Having pulled them all out, they went before the king together and said:
"Does Your Majesty not know for yourself that what you have done is unjust, and that your actions have brought greed and harm upon the myriad people?"
"Depart from this country at once; otherwise, you will surely harm one another.

Upon hearing this, the king was struck with great terror and trembled so violently that the hair on his body stood on end. He departed the country by means of chariots and cavalry, and in his state of extreme distress, he wove grass mats to sell for his livelihood.
The ministers and the people took the king’s younger brother and enthroned him as king; he then governed uprightly and did not oppress the myriad subjects.
When King Jie heard that his brother had risen and was about to become king, he felt inward joy and thought to himself:
"I can ask my brother for something so that I may sustain myself."
He then submitted a petition, detailing his circumstances in full, and begged the king for a single district where he might provide for himself.
The king immediately granted it, feeling pity for his distress; having obtained one district, he governed it with integrity.
He then begged for two districts, then four, five, and up to ten.
Twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, up to a hundred villages;
two hundred up to five hundred villages;
he then requested half the kingdom, which the king immediately granted him, and he governed it properly.

After such a long time, Jie gave rise to greedy thoughts and immediately mobilized half the army of his own country to attack his brother’s state; he was victorious and thus regained his former kingdom.
Again, a thought arose in him:
"Why now do I not mobilize the entire army of my country to attack two states, three states, or four states?"
He then went forth to attack them and achieved complete victory, subsequently bringing the four kingdoms under his rightful governance.
Again, a thought arose in him:
"Why should I not now raise the armies of these four kingdoms to attack the fifth kingdom?"
He then went forth to attack and immediately achieved victory once more.

At that time, the land was completely exhausted and all within the four seas came under the King's dominion; he then changed his title and established himself as the Great Victorious King (Mahājayarāja).
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then tested him to see whether he knew contentment.

He transformed himself into a young brahmin of the Kauśika clan, wishing to see the king; with his hair disheveled, leaning on a golden staff and holding a golden pitcher, he stood at the palace gate.
The gatekeeper addressed the king, saying:
"Outside there is a brahmin of the Kauṇḍinya clan who wishes to see the king.
The king said:
"Very well," [the king] replied.
He then invited him to sit before him, and after exchanging greetings and inquiries of courtesy, he said to the king:
"I have recently come from the seashore, where I saw a great kingdom of abundance and joy, with a flourishing population and many precious treasures; you should go and attack it."
When the king confirmed his satisfaction and further desired to obtain this kingdom, the king said,
"I truly desire to have it.
The Heavenly King then spoke to him:
"You should prepare the ships and raise an army to await me; seven days from now, I shall lead the King there.
As soon as he had spoken, the Heavenly King vanished.
On that day, he mobilized a great army and prepared his ships even more extensively, yet he did not see the brahmin coming.
At that time, the king was filled with sorrow and distress; he struck his thigh and said:
"Alas! What a tragedy!"
"I have now lost this great kingdom, like gaining the horse of the Kaurava but failing to hold it firmly; as expected, it has returned and is no longer seen.
At that time, the people of the entire nation turned their seats toward the king; when the king wept, they wept too, and when the king grieved, they grieved too.
The king, dwelling in sorrow that never ceased, heard and recognized these verses from the sutra; thereupon, a thought arose in his mind and he spoke, saying:
"Increasing mindfulness follows desire; Having already attained it, one further aspires for more. Day by day it grows, becoming a source of joy, And from this, one attains mastery."
The King then explained the meaning of the verses on desire for the assembly, offering one thousand gold coins to anyone who could interpret the meaning of these verses.
At that time, there was a youth in the assembly named Udaya.
Udāyin immediately said to the king:
"I am able to explain this meaning; please grant me seven days, and then I shall return to respond.
When the seven days had passed, he said to his mother:
"I now wish to go to the king's presence to dispel his sorrow.
His mother said to her son:
"My son, do not go for now. The affairs of a sovereign are as difficult as handling burning fire; his commands are like a sharp blade, and he is difficult to approach."
The son said:
"Mother, do not grieve. By my own power, I can master the meaning of the King's verses; you shall receive a generous reward, with which we may enjoy ourselves to our heart's content."
He then went before the king and said,
"I have now come to address this matter.
He immediately spoke these verses:
"Increasing mindfulness according to one's desires, having already attained yet wishing for more, letting go without restraint—like a thirsty person drinking hot soup.
Even if one were to fill the entire world with horses, gold, and silver, one would never be satisfied; only the wise practice correctly."
Just as horns grow, increasing day by day, so it is with human beings: they do not perceive their own increasing desire.
Hunger and thirst are never-ending; they recur day after day.
Even if one were to obtain a mountain of gold reaching to the heavens, shaped like Mount Sumeru, one would still find no satiety—unless one possesses wisdom and practices the right path.
I have never heard of one who sought to reach the dark realm of suffering; I wish to hear about the distancing from desire.
He who is weary of desire is wise; weariness with desire is supreme, for the outflows of desire are difficult to leave behind.
The wise person perceives suffering and does not follow craving; like one making a wheel, they can ensure it is firm.
Gradually abandoning desire, the mind gradually attains peace. Desiring to attain the stability of the Path, they completely relinquish all that is desired.
The king said: "I understand your intention.

I have governed the entire world, and there is no place within the four seas that does not submit to my rule; even this should be enough for satisfaction, yet you still desire the distant lands beyond the sea."
King Mahājayanta then said to Uttara:
"Young man, if you are well-disposed, rely upon the Honored One of the world.
You have spoken of desire as being most painful; your wisdom is indeed such."
"You have recited eight verses; for each verse, I offer a thousand coins, which I wish to present to you, Venerable One, as these explanations of the meaning are most compassionate.
Utpalā replied in verse:
"I do not need these treasures; take them so that you may provide for yourself."
Finally, he spoke in verse, his mind far removed from sensual pleasures:
"My mother, the Great Queen, is frail and aged; Desiring to repay her kindness, I give her a thousand gold coins To enable her to provide for herself."
"King Mahājayanta then offered one thousand gold coins so that she might provide for the old woman.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"The one who was King Mahājayanta at that time was none other than this brāhmaṇa who sows rice."
The youth Udaya at that time was none other than myself.
At that time, I also dispelled the pain and grief of this brahmin; now, having completely severed all such pain and grief of this brahmin, I shall never again be attached to suffering.

The Buddha, based on these original causes, expounded the meaning of this fascicle so that I, a later student, might hear this teaching and compose verses to serve as an illumination for future generations, ensuring that my sutras and Dharma remain long in the world.
*Arthavargīya Sūtra*:
"Increasing mindfulness according to one's desire, having already attained it, one further aspires; increasing daily, one takes joy in it and attains mastery."
There are those who crave worldly desires; sitting amidst greed and delusion, they have lost their aspiration for the Dharma, and the poisoned arrow has struck their bodies.
This desire should be shunned as one would the head of a venomous snake; turning away from what the world delights in, one should practice meditation with steadfast concentration.

Those who sow treasures in the fields, those who raise oxen and horses, and those who sit among women bound by desire—acting out of folly, they violate their own persons; being weak, they act as if strong;
through their servitude, they incur great enmity, and subsequently suffer pain in the darkness, like a ship wrecked at sea.
"Therefore, it is said: 'Gather your mind, stay far from desire, and do not transgress; strive diligently for liberation, and board the ship to reach the shore.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning, the bhikṣus rejoiced.
The Sūtra of King Udayana, Number Two. Thus have I heard:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in a clay cell among the rocks in the country of Kośala, with long hair, beard, and nails, wearing tattered robes.

At that time, King Udayana, wishing to go out for an excursion, arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. His attendant immediately ordered the roads and bridges to be repaired, and upon returning, reported to the king:
"The roads have been prepared; Your Majesty may depart."
The king, accompanied only by his beautiful women and court jesters, rode to Mount Yijie (Mount Ajañña) and dismounted to proceed on foot.

One of the beautiful women was walking through the mountains, moving from one crag to another, when she saw between some rocks a stone hut where a bhikkhu sat with long hair, beard, and nails, his robes tattered and torn, appearing like a ghost. She then cried out loudly to the prince:
"There is a ghost in there!"
"There is a ghost within this place.
The King then asked from afar:
"Where is it located?"
The beautiful woman said, "He is nearby, in an earthen chamber among the rocks.
The king immediately drew his sword and followed her; seeing the bhikṣu in such a state, he asked:
“What kind of person are you?
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa.”
The king asked,
"What kind of śramaṇa are you?
He replied:
“I am a śramaṇa of the Śākyas.
The king asked,
“Are you an arhat?”
He said: "No.
[The other asked: "Are there four dhyānas?"
He spoke again:
"There is none. [The other asked:
"Is it perhaps the third dhyāna or the second dhyāna?"
He spoke again:
“No. “Would you go as far as the first dhyāna?”
He replied, "In truth, he practices the first dhyāna.

The king was then incensed and, unable to understand this, looked toward his attendant eunuch with a lustful thought, thinking, "This śramaṇa is but a vulgar man without true practice; how could he have seen my beautiful woman? He then commanded his attendant:
"Quickly take the broken string and cut it off to bind this man.
The attendant then went away.
The mountain deity thought:
"This bhikṣu is without fault; he is now about to die by the hand of his enemy.
I shall protect him and cause him to escape this calamity.
He then transformed himself into the body of a great boar and walked slowly toward the king.
The attendant immediately informed the king:
"A large pig is close by, right next to Your Majesty.
The king then abandoned the bhikṣu and drew his sword to pursue the pig.

When the bhikṣu saw that the king had gone far away, he ran out and reached the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, at Śrāvastī, where he recounted the matter from beginning to end to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus then reported it to the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha, based on this very foundation, manifested the arising of meaningful existence and commanded me, a bhikṣu, to fully understand the words emerging from the sūtra scrolls, so as to provide illumination for those who study in future generations and ensure that my sūtra-dharma remains long in the world.
At that time, the Buddha spoke the *Arthavargīya-sūtra*:
"Bound by many wishes, One dwells obstructed by what is false;
Because of these obstructions, one is far from the Right Path, And the mind of desire makes wisdom difficult to attain."
Sitting, one may bind the womb; binding to form is firm and difficult to untie.
If one does not contemplate the nature of coming and going, wisdom alone can sever this root.
With greed and desire, one is blinded by ignorance, unaware that the benefits of the wrong path increase.
Sitting here, one is about to be overcome by pain and sorrow; from this point on, what can one rely upon?
A person in life should realize this: the world’s perversities are difficult to rely upon.
Abandoning the right path and clinging to delusive thoughts, one’s life is short and death is very near.
Successive cycles are the suffering of this world; the stream of desire flows through birth and death.
At the time of death, one then remembers one's grievances; following desire, the condemnation of the womb is extreme.
One may receive a body of pain, like a fish in a dwindling stream whose flow has been cut off.
Since it is acceptable to sever the body through insight, what more could be added regarding the three periods of time?
With effort and desire toward both sides, one should awaken to that which is appropriate and not become attached;
do not act in a way that brings self-reproach, and do not defile yourself through what you see or hear.
"Awakened through contemplative insight, he crossed the ocean; He did not conceive of a self, yet honored the noble ones.
Through diligent practice, he pulled out those who had not yet emerged, thereby bringing them to a state free from doubt.
When the Buddha had spoken this Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning, the bhikṣus rejoiced.
3. The Sūtra on Sudarśana. Thus have I heard:

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where he was honored and revered by kings, ministers, and householders. They served him with unwearied devotion, providing him with whatever was required: food and drink, clothing and bedding, and medicine for illness.
At that time, the brahmins sat together in their lecture hall and deliberated, saying:
"We were formerly treated with honor by kings, ministers, commoners, and householders; now they have abandoned us and no longer employ us."
"They have all turned to serve the śramaṇa Gautama and his disciples; now we must together devise a stratagem to defeat them.
They then deliberated:
"We should now seek out the most beautiful and excellent women from among our own ranks to kill him together, and bury his corpse within the Jeta Grove."

Thus, you will bring disgrace upon the śramaṇa Gautama and his disciples, causing their ill repute to spread far and wide; those who once attended to them will distance themselves and no longer show them respect.
"None of these scholars shall receive any more food or clothing; they must all come to serve us.
We shall then become the World-Honored Ones and destroy Gautama, for there is no one in the world who can surpass us."
They then went together, and Suśīma said to them:

"Do you not know that we have now been abandoned and will no longer be employed? Yet you have instead taken the śramaṇa Gautama as your teacher; can you truly be indignant and act for the benefit of the assembly?"
Suśīma asked, "What is meant by 'acting for one's own benefit'?
He replied:
"Only by relinquishing my life-span shall I die.
He replied, "I cannot do so."
He said, "If you cannot do so, from this day forward, I shall never again include you among my ranks.
Hearing this, the woman was deeply distressed and immediately replied, "I agree."
"This is my duty," he said.
The assembly of students replied,
"Excellent!"
They then instructed their daughter together, saying:
"From this day forward, go to the Buddha's dwelling morning and evening; frequent the Jeta Grove repeatedly so that all the people may see and know you."
"In this way, we shall join together to kill you and bury you among the Śāla trees, so that Gautama may suffer humiliation.

The young girl immediately followed these instructions; she went back and forth to the śramaṇa’s location several times to let everyone know that the girl was in such a state, and then they seized her, killed her, and buried her among the Śāla trees.
The many brahmins gathered together and went to the gate of the royal palace, voicing their grievances:
"Among our students there was a daughter who was uniquely beautiful, peerless in her complexion; she has now passed away, and we do not know her whereabouts."
The king asked,
"Where do you girls usually go and come from?
They replied together:
"I always go to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama.
The king said,
"In that case, you should seek it from him."
He then requested soldiers from the king, who granted them at once.

Seeking him out, they traveled on until they reached the Jeta Grove, where they dug up the corpse, placed it upon a bed, and carried it together through the four main roads of Śrāvastī. They went through every street and alley, crying out in grievance:

"Look at this śramaṇa Gautama, the son of the Śākyas! He constantly proclaims his virtue and precepts as vast, universal, and unsurpassed; yet how could he have secretly consorted with a woman and buried her after killing her?"
"What dharma, what virtue, or what conduct of precepts could such people as these possibly possess?
At mealtime, the bhikṣus all took up their alms-bowls and entered the city to beg for food. When the householders and citizens saw them from afar, they reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas claim for themselves that they possess dharma, virtue, and precepts; yet the offenses committed by this lot of yours are like this—what goodness could there possibly be in them?"
"How can we obtain food and clothing again?

Hearing this, the bhikṣus took their empty alms-bowls, went out of the city to wash their hands and feet, and having secured their bowls, they went to the Buddha's dwelling. They paid homage and stood together without sitting down, recounting the matter in detail.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Though others speak with idle thoughts, falsehoods, and reckless words, Or provoke a crowd to fight while enduring the pain of arrows—
When hearing such vulgar speech, whether good or evil, A bhikṣu remains patient, his mind undisturbed."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall be subject to this false slander for no more than seven days.

At that time, there was a laywoman of pure faith named Weiyán. Having heard in the city that the bhikṣus had returned empty-handed from their almsround, she felt profound contempt for [the situation] and turned her thoughts toward the Buddha and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus. She then proceeded quickly to Jeta’s Grove, arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, circumambulated him, and sat to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma extensively for them. When it was finished, Yama rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha:
"I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation to take a meal at my home for seven days."
The Buddha accepted his request by remaining silent; Vimalakīrti then circumambulated the Buddha three times and departed.
When seven days had passed, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, shall enter the city and recite this verse throughout the alleys, lanes, and streets at the four crossroads."
"Constantly deceiving and inverted in delusion, they claim that acting with the body incurs no offense;
yet they are fully equipped for heavy, dark deeds of deception.
Reaching that suffering through their own resentment, they fail to cultivate the factors of the noble path and do not restrain themselves, becoming thieves to their own souls."
Harsh words cut off the very root; one should always guard the gate of the senses.
To disparage those who are worthy is to bring about ruin; to hold those empty of virtue in high esteem brings no merit.
From the mouth, manifold anxieties enter; through a jealous heart, the multitude finds no peace.
Seizing and plundering the wealth of others, or using force to deceive them—these may indeed be achieved;
yet all such acts can be endured, for they are the very means by which one loses one's treasures.
To harbor resentment toward a person of integrity is the sixth of the worldly faults; the remaining five are as follows.
"How could there be a path leading there? It is because his mind was settled in improper conduct;
he has been deceived by a hundred thousand [sins].
Ānanda immediately received these instructions and entered the city together with him, preaching in the lanes, alleys, and at the four crossroads exactly as the Buddha had spoken.
At that moment, the people of Śrāvastī and the inhabitants of all the households conceived this thought:
"The son of the Śākya clan is truly without evil; having been trained in the Śākya household, he will never engage in unwholesome conduct."
At that time, a group of various brahmins were disputing among themselves in the lecture hall.
One man among them spoke of the matter concerning the group of the son of Lulu, shouting out as he left:
"You lot killed Hao-shou yourselves, yet you harbor resentment toward the Buddha and his disciples!"
When the minister heard these words, he entered and informed the king.
The king immediately summoned the assembly of brahmins and asked:
"Did you all conspire together to kill Bhadraśiras?"
He then replied,
"It is indeed so.
The king said in anger:
"How can they, within the borders of my kingdom, claim to be followers of the Way while harboring murderous intent? They must be severely punished!
He then commanded his attendants:
"Arrest all these followers of the Way."
Having searched throughout every street and alley of the city of Śrāvastī, they drove him out beyond the borders of the kingdom.
At the time for the meal, the Buddha, accompanied by his bhikṣus, all carrying their alms-bowls, entered the city.
At that time, there was a lay follower named Aśvali who, seeing the Buddha from afar, went to pay his respects and cried out to the Buddha:

"Those who hear this do not recognize the names of the four directions and their hearts are filled with great sorrow; they can no longer recite the sutras and dharmas they have heard, and upon hearing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus have been slandered by evil reputations, they are overcome with resentment."
The Buddha said to Āśvalāyana,
"It is not that there is no karmic cause and condition from a past life.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"One is reviled for speaking little; one is also reviled for speaking much.
One is reviled for speaking with loyalty; there is no evil in the world that does not revile.
This was so in the past, will be so in the future, and exists so in the present."
"Who could ever see such a one disparaged throughout their entire life? Even for as long as they live, it would be difficult to find anyone more worthy of reverence.
The Buddha extensively preached the sutra for the Asura, then proceeded to the house of Sudatta and sat directly upon the central seat.
Sudatta then prostrated himself before the Buddha and, with palms joined, said:

"I was recently overcome by grief; I lost my sense of direction and could no longer recite the sutras and teachings I had heard. Now I hear that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus have been slandered with an evil reputation."
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"I am like an elephant in battle; Though wounded, I harbor no resentment.
I maintain this patient mind, While the people of the world lack such joyful intent."
"My hands have no sores; though I carry poison in my hands, no poison arises from what is not a sore.
Thus, when one acts with goodness, evil does not come to pass.
The Buddha extensively preached the sūtra for Sudatta and then proceeded to the house of Viśākhā, where he sat directly upon the central seat.
Having finished paying his respects, Vimala joined his palms and said:

"Just now I was overcome with grief; I lost my sense of direction and could no longer recite the sutras and teachings I had heard. Now I hear that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus have been slandered by an evil reputation."
The Buddha then spoke this verse for the sake of Vemacitra:
"To try to vex one who is unenlightened and free from desire— With inner purity, how could the outside be defiled?
The fool, harboring resentment, brings harm upon himself; It is like blowing fine dust against the wind."

At that time, Viyaya had finished eating his meal with the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; he provided them with water for rinsing their mouths and sat in the lower seats to listen to the Buddha’s discourse on the sūtras.

Then the King spoke this verse:
"Now, as one of the three who are valiant and wise, you bow your head at the feet of the All-Seeing One.
At your first birth, you shook heaven and earth; sitting beneath the tree’s shade, your body remained unexposed."
At that time, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power and descended before the assembly of bhikṣus, who all took their seats.
The Śākyas and the Śākya women all prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and each took their respective seats.
The King also took his seat and praised the Buddha in verse,
saying: "Riding an elephant, a horse, or a golden chariot, Traveling among the palace halls and pavilions,
With golden feet treading upon the ground— How could calluses ever form on such feet?"
The bases of supernormal power are my chariot, its range boundless according to my will;
riding this wondrous and subtle vehicle, how could the worldly chariot endure for long?
Clad in fine, soft garments, one’s physical form appears beautiful once dressed.
Walking with a body covered in golden dew—what excellence is there in such clothing?
The King’s Law is my garment; mindful of the world, I practice the teachings.
This garment was fashioned by those who have trained before; I have awakened as a Tathāgata.
Formerly you dwelt in lofty palaces, building pavilions at will;
now you sleep alone among the trees—what reliance can you have against fear?
O Gautama, you are without enmity in this world; having severed the roots of hatred and lust, you are free from them.
Freed from desire and free from sorrow, having no enemy, what should one fear?
Formerly, one feasted on savory flavors, eating fragrant delicacies from golden vessels;
today one has obtained this food—what joy is there in such coarse and vile fare?
I first partook of the flavor of the Dharma-food, Abandoning greed and following the path of suffering and emptiness;
Having completely severed the roots of the four kinds of food, I wander for alms out of compassion for the world.
The Honored One bathes in fragrant flowers, And a troupe of singing girls follows him with music.
Dwelling amidst the trees on Mount Udena, who is it that bathes in the Clear One?
Taking the Dharma and the precepts as his river, purity and wisdom are both contained therein.
Having exhausted all strife, he goes to bathe in purity; having crossed over by wandering, he shall not return again.

At that time, the Buddha extensively expounded the Dharma for the king and the Śākya women. He first manifested the practice of giving and the observance of precepts, briefly explaining the path to the heavens; he skillfully described the suffering of the realms of pain and led them toward the realization of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are the immediate relatives of the world, through which one may attain peace and suchness.

With his enlightened mind, the Buddha knew that King Śuddhodana’s heart was filled with joy, that his nature was gentle, and that he was free from the bonds of distraction; thus, knowing he could be taught the Dharma of skillful deliverance, he spoke of the Truth of Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, the king attained understanding while still seated; the defilements of the three poisons were removed, and he gained the eye of truth within the Dharma. It was just as when a clean silk cloth is cast into dye—it immediately takes on a beautiful color—and so it was with the king’s entry into the Dharma.
At that time, the king, having seen the Truth and severed his doubts, attained understanding within the Dharma. He rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and with palms joined, said:

"I have drawn near and drawn near; I have distanced myself and distanced myself. Now I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Bhikṣus. Accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*); for as long as life lasts, I shall remain entirely pure and commit no transgressions."
Thus, among the Śākyas there were those who took refuge in the Buddha, those who took refuge in the Dharma, and those who took refuge in the Saṃgha;
the women of the Śākya clan likewise took refuge in the same manner.

Among them, some observed the precept against killing, some observed the precept against stealing, some observed the precept against sexual misconduct, some observed the precept against lying, and some observed the precept of abstaining from intoxicants by staying far from wine and not drinking it.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having clearly perceived the Dharma and being free from doubt regarding the realization of the Truths, became courageous in the Dharma. He then rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him with these verses of meaningful feet: "What should one who is fully endowed with precepts perceive? What should one who is fully endowed with concentration perceive? What should one who is fully endowed with wisdom perceive? What should one who is fully endowed with liberation perceive?
What should one who is fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation perceive?"
The one who speaks says that suffering arises from the aggregates.
I pray that Gautama will explain this for me. You who have been born as a Hero of the World, your mind is set on the Right Path;
you have already cast off heavy resentment through your past conduct, and you do not cling to future desires.
One does not grasp at the present as it comes, nor does one accept the emptiness of honor;
one does not cling with craving to perceptions of the future, nor does one grieve over perceptions of the distant past.
One traveling a long distance may abandon fine and soft things; when false views are exhausted, they become non-existent.
Having departed from fear, one has no dread; one’s faith is unshakable and free from doubt.
Free from envy, one delights in giving to others;
practicing such love for the life of the Noble One, one is able to maintain self-restraint and harbor few expectations. Having attained much wisdom, one is free from envy.
Neither loathsome nor unattractive, neither garrulous nor seductive; Free from double-tongued speech, abandoning frivolity and doubt, the mind is entirely liberated and without attachment.
Having cast aside self-view and abandoned ornate falsehoods, one proceeds with composure and is able to resolve oppositions; Nor does one seek to forcibly sever the thought of desire.
One does not learn by seeking what is desired; there is nothing at all, nor is there any sorrow.
Free from resentment and having abandoned craving, one is not made subject to the flavors of the senses.
Do not exalt yourself as being peerless; when encountering slander, take it upon yourself to receive respect.
One should practice the contemplation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, for seeing good and evil is not a matter of mere expectation.
Departing from wherever one is, there is no place of abiding; observing the nature of phenomena, what should one cling to?
Desire and form are empty, and even formlessness is absent; following clever calculations, one does not seek liberation.
When craving has already ceased, one is then at rest; the three realms are empty, and there is no intent for pleasure.
How can one fully understand detachment?
By crossing the ocean from whence many sorrows arise.
One does not wish for birth or the sight of having children; rather, one should increase the jewels of the earth through the practice of vows.
Coming, it is not born; going, it does not arrive. What could one seek, and from where could it be obtained?
There is nowhere to which it can be said to go. Let all the śramaṇas who study direct their minds toward this:
let them seek its location, and they will understand how it departs as if by physical contact.
Neither envious nor greedy, though in a position of high honor, one finds no delight;
finding no delight in the middle or low states, one abandons what arises from the Dharma that is contrary to the Dharma.
All these are empty and non-existent; neither attained nor sought after.
"Do not desire worldly, perverse pleasures; when the mind has come to rest, one reaches the end [of suffering].
When the Buddha had finished preaching this *Arthavargīya Sūtra*, the bhikṣus, King Śuddhodana, and the people of the Śākya clan were all filled with joy.
16. The Sūtra on King Vīrūḍhaka. Thus have I heard:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu had recently constructed a great hall that was not yet long finished. All the Śākyas spoke together, saying:
"From this day forward, let no śramaṇa, brahmin, member of the Śākya clan wearing the cap and robe, nor the son of an elder, enter this hall before us."
"First let the Buddha enter, next the community of bhikṣus, and only then shall the other people follow behind.
At that time, Prince Vairāṭa of Śrāvastī arrived at the kingdom of the Śākyas on business; before he had even reached the city, he went to stay overnight in the newly constructed palace.
Tomorrow we shall enter the city; once we have finished what we intend to take, we will return to our own country.
When the Śākyas heard that Prince Viśvantara was staying overnight in the new palace, they were greatly displeased. Their anger did not subside, and they cried out in abuse:
"How can you now allow this servant's son to enter this palace first?"
They then dug up the earth within the palace to a depth of seven feet and discarded it; they took fresh soil to restore the site and further took cow’s milk to wash the four palaces.

When Prince Lūli heard that the Śākyas were speaking unkindly and ill of him, he dug seven feet of earth from within the palace and replaced it with fresh soil; he then washed the four palaces entirely with milk, yet he further reviled me, calling me a slave-girl for defiling this new palace.
Hearing of his internal distress and his sorrowful attachment to the kingdom, [the ministers] thought, "When I later take over the administration of the state, how shall I govern the Śākyas?
Not long after this, the King of Śrāvastī passed away; the ministers assembled for consultation and summoned the crown prince to be enthroned as king.
King Lūli then asked his attendant ministers:
"When there is an impure and wicked king of a nation, to what extent does his transgression reach?
The attendant ministers replied:
"Such a crime leads to death.
The king said, "It is so."

"The Śākyas find me impure and wicked; yet the Śākyas are the Buddha's own kinsmen. Even if the Buddha were to harbor such affection for the Śākyas that he could not bring himself to punish his own sons for their crimes, [I would still act]."
The ministers immediately replied, "The Buddha has renounced worldly desires and harbors no affection for his kinsmen; therefore, there will be no difficulty in punishing the Śākyas for their crimes.
When the king heard this report, he immediately issued an edict to mobilize the fourfold army.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, they marched out of the city raising their banners, intending to attack the city of Kapilavastu.

At the time for the meal, the Buddha took his alms bowl and entered Śrāvastī to seek food; having finished eating, he left the city and descended onto the road, where there was a śāla tree with sparse branches and little shade. He stood beneath it and gazed out.

The king set out with his army along the main road and saw from afar the Buddha sitting beneath a tree providing sparse shade. He immediately alighted from his carriage and approached the Buddha; having completed his prostrations, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Yes."

Now there are other great trees here with flourishing branches and leaves that provide abundant shade; these great trees are called *kacchānā*. In Kapilavastu, there are many *udumbara* and *nyagrodha* trees. Why does the Buddha not sit in their shade?
"Why do you sit beneath this small śāla tree?
It has few branches and leaves; how can there be any coolness under a tree that provides no shade?
The Buddha replied:
"Because they love its name and delight in its coolness, they sit beneath it.
The King thought to himself:
"If this is so, the Buddha still maintains affection for the Śākyas and continues to have a supportive intention toward them."
He immediately withdrew his troops from that place and returned to his own country.

The Buddha instructed the people of Śrāvastī; then, desiring to go to the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he set out with the bhikṣus and arrived at the land of the Śākyas, where he gave instruction within the Nyagrodha Garden.
After some time, the King of Śrāvastī again asked his ministers and attendants:
"If there were an impure and wicked king, what would be the extent of his offense?"
The ministers replied,
"Such a crime merits the death penalty.
The king spoke again:
“The Śākyas have brought evil upon me; yet you, my children, are all close kinsmen of the Buddha. The Buddha must surely have regard for the Śākyas, and thus I shall never defeat you, my children.”
The ministers spoke again, saying:
"We have all heard the words of the śramaṇas:
'Gautama has already severed his lust.'"
"What affection or love could there be for such close kinsmen?
If the King wishes to punish them for their crimes, it shall not be difficult.
When the King heard these reports from his ministers, he immediately ordered the mobilization of the fourfold army and led the host out of the city, arriving at the kingdom of the Śākyas.
When they had traveled until nightfall, they stayed overnight at a place forty *li* from the city of Śrāvastī.

All the Śākyas heard that the King of Śrāvastī had mobilized a fourfold army and intended to come and attack their country; being only several tens of *li* from the city, they feared he would arrive by the following day. They immediately dispatched swift messengers on horseback to the Buddha’s location, saying:
"We pray that the Buddha will instruct us as to what expedient means we should employ."
The Buddha then addressed the Śākyas:
"Keep the city gates firmly closed; the King will ultimately be unable to achieve victory.
Should he open the gates and enter, King Lur-le will undoubtedly slaughter all the Śākyas."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the rider prostrated to the Buddha and departed on his horse as he had come.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was standing behind the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

“O One of Clear Wisdom, do not be concerned for the Śākyas. I could now lift up the entire Śākya kingdom and transport it to another world-system; even if one were to enclose it within an iron cage, what could all the inhabitants of the world together possibly do about it?”
The Buddha then addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Even if you were able to do so, what would you do with his transgression?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"But one can only speak of matters with form; what can be done about formless offenses?
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Good and evil deeds never rot; From merit comes happiness, while from darkness comes suffering."
"Good and evil sprouts turn toward the rising sun; for a long time past, the body has been their dwelling place.
King Śrāvastī immediately polished his weapons and armor, and together they advanced to attack the city of the Śākyas.
All the Śākyas together raised the fourfold army—
elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry— and also went out from the city, intending to resist King Virūḍhaka.
The Śākyas likewise polished their weapons, intending to fight against the King of Śrāvastī and his army.

Before they had even seen one another, the Śākyas drew their bows and shot sharp-edged arrows that severed chariots; they likewise shot and severed yokes, shot and severed hubs, cut through axles, and shot and severed the necks of horses. They also shot and severed human bodies and precious jewels, yet caused no injury.
The King of Śrāvastī was seized with great terror and turned to his attendants, asking:
"Do you not know that the Śākyas have already gone out of the city to meet us in battle and die? We shall never achieve victory; it would be better for us to return early."
The attendant ministers immediately said to the king:
"We previously reported that we have heard all the Śākyas uphold the five precepts and do not violate them for as long as they live."
"From birth until the time of death, one must not dare to cause harm; to cause harm is to violate the precepts, whereas by simply advancing [in virtue], one may achieve victory."
The king immediately led his troops forward and broke through the Śākya ranks.
Seeing the king advancing so forcefully, the Śākyas entered the city and closed the gates.
At that time, the King of Śrāvastī sent a messenger to speak to the Śākyas:
"What enmity do you, my uncle, have with me that you will not open your gate?
I merely wish to borrow something and shall depart the city immediately without lingering.
Those among the Śākyas who believed the Buddha’s words, whose fundamental practice was the Dharma and Vinaya, and who were without doubt regarding the Path, then said:
"There is no need to open the door.

Śreṇika had not yet purified his mind; though he had taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, he lacked certainty and harbored doubts. Thinking it appropriate to open the door, he spoke again:
"We may not do this; I fear there is an adversary within."
"We shall all sit together as elders and cast lots. Those who do not take a lot shall be considered unwilling to bring the king inside;
those who take a lot shall be considered willing to bring the king inside.
Whichever side is in the majority, I, too, shall accordingly follow their course."
"Those who have received the tally and those who have not are few indeed.
The crowd said,
"We must open the gate and let the King in."

The Śākyas then opened the gates and let him in; just as King Virūḍhaka entered the city of Kapilavastu, he immediately seized the Śākyas, intending to take them out of the city and put them to death.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra said to King Śrāvastī:
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me a small boon.
The king replied:
"What wish do you have, General?
"I wish that while I am submerged in this pool for a moment, by that time all the Śākyas may emerge from the city and flee."
The ministers said to him,
"Your Majesty should grant Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s wish, so that he may remain within the water for as long as he desires.
The king then granted him his wish.
Śreṇika Mānava immediately sank into the pond, wrapped his hair around the roots of a tree, and died.
The King, wondering why he had remained in the water for so long, sent a messenger to investigate:
"What was Śreṇika Mānava doing in the water?"
"As Your Majesty commanded, we went to investigate and saw that Śreṇika was dead at the bottom of the water.
We have returned to inform Your Majesty:
'O King, do you know? Śreṇika wrapped his hair around the roots of a tree and died.'"
The king immediately had the remaining Śākyas in the city strangled, and asked again:
"Are all those born as Śākyas now dead?
The minister replied: "Yes."
"They have all been trampled to death by elephants.
The king then returned to his kingdom from that place.
At the hour of *bhūṣa*, the Buddha addressed all the bhikṣus:
"Let us go together to the Śivaka-Ṣaḍvargika Lecture Hall.
All the bhikṣus replied, "Yes."

The Buddha, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to the Śvetavyūha Lecture Hall; on the way, he passed by the places where the Śākyas had died. Among the Śākyas, there were still some who were able to speak, and seeing the Buddha from afar, they raised their voices crying out in grievance. Hearing the cries of the Śākyas, the Buddha was filled with profound and piercing sorrow.
The Buddha then said to the bhikṣus, "The transgression committed by the foolish man Vairūḍaka is no small matter.
The Buddha then went to the territory of the Śākyas and manifested countless natural seats; the Buddha and the bhikṣus all sat upon them.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma extensively for the Śākyas, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "What do you think?

If a butcher performs such work and makes his living by such means, could he, by reason of those causes and conditions, ever obtain the joy of riding upon a noble elephant, a divine horse, or a chariot of the seven treasures?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“Never. The Buddha said:
“Excellent! The mind is also like this: one does not see or hear that by such an occupation as slaughtering, one can establish oneself in wealth and happiness. Why is this?
"The butcher lacks a heart of compassion or a mind of pity, for he observes and divines among the various beasts.
The Buddha spoke again: "Bhikṣus!"

"What do you think, my friends? Do those who are fishermen, hunters, and cattle-slaughterers—performing such deeds and engaging in such occupations as their means of livelihood—ever get to ride divine elephants, noble horses, or precious chariots, enjoying wealth and pleasure to their heart's content?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“Never. The Buddha said:
“Excellent! I too have neither heard of nor seen fishermen, hunters, or ox-slaughterers who, by living through such occupations, were able to attain wealth and happiness. Why is this? Because...”
"Your son, Cao Yuan'ai, lacks compassion and insight; he uses divination to distance himself from joy—how can this be called the Way?

This foolish man even harms those who are progressing toward the Way and have attained its fruits. Now I know that this son is also far removed from goodness; as soon as he is born, he shall witness his own downfall, and in seven days, he shall be swept away by the waters."
“Monks! For this reason, you should maintain a mind of loving-kindness; do not train in a mind of harm. Even when seeing others being burned or wronged, do not give rise to thoughts of injury.

The Buddha, based on this foundation, for these causes and conditions, and arising from this principle, caused his disciples to fully understand it as a formal discourse for their instruction, so as to provide illumination for future generations and ensure that my teachings and the Way remain long in the world.
At that time, the Buddha spoke this Sūtra of Meaningful Verses:
"From a lack of compassion comes fear; Through successive human lives, listen with discernment.
Now I shall speak of matters that cause distress, That which I have abandoned out of dread."
The suffering that revolves around us is common to all people in the world, like fish in a dried-up stream whose flow has been cut off.
While dwelling in suffering, they give rise to the intent to harm; may I, in their stead, dispel their fears and the darkness of ignorance through bliss.
The entire world is thus scorched; throughout the ten directions all is in turmoil with no peace.
Due to self-conceit, they do not abandon craving; because they do not see [the truth], they maintain a mind of delusion.
Do not create bonds that seek out dark suffering; I observe all such intentions as being unpleasant.
They lead to painful torment and the sight of thorns, for the cessation of views is difficult to endure.
From the piercing thorn he did not abandon his firm resolve; carrying the thorn, he wandered throughout the entire world.
Now that the Honored One has seen and extracted the painful thorn, he no longer dwells on suffering and shall no longer wander.
In this world, one should not accept anything at all; abandon the root of perverse confusion and do not rely upon it.
One should find weariness with desire and cross over all things; by training to avoid suffering, one transcends and achieves self-perfection.
Abide in sincerity and do not speak falsely; maintain upright conduct and empty yourself of double-tongued speech.
Extinguish the fire of hatred and scatter greed; abandon affliction and attain the vision of wisdom.
Cast off dullness and do not lie in sleep; stay far from those who lack liberation and do not associate with them.
Do not take up what is foul and loathsome; let thoughts of attachment to emptiness be utterly extinguished.
Do not be led astray by deception; when encountering forms, do not be enslaved by them.
Knowing that this exquisite body is not to be clung to, do not seek liberation through the play of the aggregates.
Cast off thoughts of the long-past and do not dwell on them; likewise, harbor no expectations for future kin.
Seeing that the present is vanishing, do not cling to sorrow; leave behind the affairs of the four seas and hasten away.
I say that greed is great, fierce, and evil; when the influxes of views enter, they breed doubt.
Bound by the mental intentions of causes and conditions, the defilement of desire ruins one and is difficult to escape.
Those who have abandoned desire are few in number; even if one were to count all those in the world, those who reach the end [of suffering] are few.
Having abandoned [desire], they do not sink nor do they flee; their stream is severed and they are free from fetters.
Having mounted the chariot of the power of truth and wisdom, one stands firm and reaches that sorrowless wisdom;
guarding against the dangers and ailments of the womb, through diligent effort and vigilance, one may attain peace.
Having reckoned that what is distant is suffering gone, one contemplates emptiness and has no attachments;
following the straight path of broad evenness, one is entirely unattached to what is seen in the world.
Since I do not even consider this small body as mine, how could I consider that which does not exist?
Since it is neither graspable nor present, and is not "mine," why should I grieve?
The root of delusion has been uprooted for the sake of purity; even if it sprouts again later, there shall be no nourishing of it.
Having already ceased to grasp at anything within, there is no need for companions, as one has abandoned the enemy.
Having abandoned all name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), one does not cling to thoughts of anything to be gathered.
Already non-existent and without location, he has no enemy in all the world;
having completely severed both perception and form, he is equal toward all that is wholesome.
Having already learned their teachings from others, one need not fear answering whatever questions arise;
this wisdom does not depend on a single fixed perspective, for that which is sought is beyond anything to be learned.
Having already renounced the absence of causes and conditions, one attains peace and reaches the vision of cessation.
Not arrogant toward those above nor fearful of those below, one dwells in equanimity where nothing is perceived.
Abiding in a pure place free from enmity and jealousy, though one may rely on views, one is not conceited because of them.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this *Arthavargīya-sūtra*, the bhikṣus were all filled with joy.
